article: How much protein does a hummus snack actually get from the dip?
Compare 45 g commercial hummus with boiled chickpeas and include the weight of a pita serving.
USDA SR Legacy commercial hummus, boiled unsalted chickpeas and whole-wheat pita. Figures are estimates for sample servings.
copy: A 45 g serving of USDA commercial hummus gives about 3.5 g protein. The same weight of plain cooked chickpeas gives about 4.0 g. The hummus entry represents a prepared dip and has more calories per gram than the chickpeas.
Put dip and bread on separate lines

A 60 g whole-wheat pita adds about 5.9 g to either version. The hummus-and-pita combination comes to around 9.4 g protein before any additional toppings. A scoop of dip does not carry the same claim as a plate of whole beans simply because both start with chickpeas.
If you know the ingredients in a homemade hummus, calculate the recipe using the weights and finished yield. The commercial reference is a different prepared food.
table: Protein from the dip, bean portion and pita

article: Does canned salmon’s protein change when you count the packing liquid?
Check which pink salmon entry represents the amount on the plate versus the whole contents.
USDA SR Legacy canned pink salmon whole contents and drained solids without skin or bones. Distinct entries, without a matched draining experiment.
related: Record the portion in the food diary
copy: The USDA pink salmon record for total can contents has 19.68 g protein per 100 g. Its drained solids without skin and bones have 24.62 g for that weight. These values apply to different edible material. Weigh the salmon after preparation if that is the portion you intend to log.
Pick the source that describes the weight

An example 90 g drained serving using the skinless, boneless reference gives about 22.2 g. A 90 g portion from the total-can reference gives about 17.7 g. Subtracting the numbers cannot tell you how much protein physically went down the drain in one can because the two records also differ in what solids they include.
Use a manufacturer label matched to the preparation where available, and keep the drained weight with the entry.
table: Protein in the two canned pink salmon references
Drained solids, without skin and bones

article: Do pumpkin or sunflower kernels add more protein to a trail mix?
Calculate an equal-weight swap between dried pumpkin kernels and dry-roasted sunflower kernels.
USDA SR Legacy dried pumpkin and squash kernels and dry-roasted sunflower kernels without salt. Extra trail-mix ingredients excluded.
copy: For 25 g of kernels, pumpkin gives about 7.6 g protein and sunflower about 4.8 g. The sunflower portion contributes about 2.8 g fiber, while the pumpkin portion gives 1.5 g in these USDA references.
Keep the amount of kernels fixed

If you replace half of a 25 g sunflower serving with pumpkin kernels, the estimate becomes 6.2 g protein. This is a change in the kernel mix, rather than an estimate for a whole bag of trail mix. Include dried fruit or chocolate individually if the finished mix matters.
The entries are hulled kernels. Seeds sold in shells have a different as-purchased weight, and salted varieties need a matching entry for a sodium comparison.
table: Protein and fiber in 25 g of trail-mix kernels

article: How do mackerel and yellowfin tuna compare when each portion provides 25 g protein?
Match protein in cooked fish and see what happens to portions and calories.
USDA SR Legacy dry-heat Atlantic mackerel and fresh yellowfin tuna cooked with dry heat. These portions are calculated, not recommendations.
copy: About 105 g cooked Atlantic mackerel or 86 g cooked yellowfin tuna provides 25 g protein using USDA values. The calculated portions are roughly 275 and 112 kcal respectively. Mackerel contains more fat in the reference, which helps explain why a similar protein amount can differ in energy.
Equal protein takes different portions of the two fish

To calculate a different target, divide the requested grams of protein by the protein per gram of the cooked fish. Use the corresponding energy value for the resulting portion. The table does not compare one species’ overall benefits or cover fish in a sauce or packing oil.
The portions are calculated examples. Pick a source for your actual kind of fish and cooked weight.
table: Cooked fish servings calculated to give about 25 g protein

article: Does roasted turkey breast offer more protein than dark chicken meat?
Compare the meat-only USDA records by cooked serving and include the fat in the same amount.
USDA SR Legacy whole turkey roasted breast meat and roasted broiler dark chicken meat. Both meat only.
copy: A 110 g portion of roasted turkey breast has about 33.1 g protein and 2.3 g fat in the USDA reference. Roasted dark chicken meat gives about 30.1 g protein and 10.7 g fat at the same cooked weight.
Use the cut on your plate

The protein difference narrows when the dark-meat serving is larger. Roughly 121 g dark chicken matches the first portion’s protein, but it still gives more total fat. Meat with skin, smoked turkey slices and ground poultry represent other foods and should be logged separately.
Weigh the edible meat without the bone or skin when using these rows. Compare seasoning and any gravy separately.
table: Cooked poultry at a matched 110 g meat-only serving

article: How much fiber does the bread add to a pita or a two-slice sandwich?
Compare an example 60 g pita with two weighed slices of commercial whole-wheat bread.
USDA SR Legacy whole-wheat pita and commercially prepared whole-wheat bread. Example two-slice weight is hypothetical.
copy: A 60 g whole-wheat pita adds about 3.7 g fiber and 5.9 g protein. Two 30 g slices of the USDA commercial whole-wheat bread reference contribute 3.6 g fiber and about 7.5 g protein. Their fiber is close at this weight, even though the bread shapes differ.
Check the total weight of the bread you will eat

If the pita is only 40 g, its fiber falls to about 2.4 g. That makes slice or pocket count a poor basis by itself. Put the filling on a separate line, especially when one sandwich has beans and the other has a meat filling.
The examples are recipe estimates. For a packaged bread, use the printed serving weight and its actual fiber value.
table: Bread contribution at a shared 60 g

article: Do lima beans or black beans add more fiber to a bowl?
Calculate protein and fiber in the same 120 g serving before you substitute cooked beans.
USDA SR Legacy large mature lima beans and mature black beans, boiled without salt. Frozen immature lima beans are outside scope.
copy: A 120 g serving of cooked black beans supplies about 10.4 g fiber, compared with 8.4 g for large mature lima beans. The black bean portion also has about 1.3 g more protein. Both USDA records describe mature beans cooked without salt.
Match mature beans to mature beans

If you swap half of the black beans for limas in a 120 g serving, the mixture gives about 9.4 g fiber and 10.0 g protein. Add the two components separately if you know their weights. Canned beans, immature lima beans and prepared bean dips have different source entries.
Use the amount of solids you ate and keep other bowl ingredients out of the bean-only comparison.
table: Two cooked bean portions and one mix

article: Does Swiss cheese add less sodium than Gouda on a sandwich?
Use equal slice weights and see whether the protein stays close.
USDA SR Legacy Gouda and Swiss cheese. Worked slices use a 25 g weight.
copy: At 25 g, the USDA Swiss cheese entry gives about 47 mg sodium. The same weight of Gouda gives about 205 mg. Both portions provide a little over 6 g protein, so the sodium comparison tells a different story from the protein numbers.
Compare the cheese before adding meat and bread

The gap is about 158 mg at the stated weight. A double 50 g Swiss portion still gives about 94 mg in this reference, while also increasing the energy and protein. These are independent cheeses and are best used as generic estimates, since salt levels vary by brand.
For a packaged slice, use the actual grams and label, especially if the product is sold as reduced sodium.
table: Cheese contribution to one sandwich at 25 g

article: How much protein is in pistachios versus macadamias?
Compare two raw 28 g portions and see the difference in total fat and protein.
USDA SR Legacy raw pistachio and macadamia nuts. Shells excluded from measured portion.
copy: A 28 g portion of raw pistachios contributes about 5.6 g protein. The same weight of raw macadamias supplies about 2.2 g. Macadamias contribute about 21.2 g fat, compared with about 12.7 g from pistachios in the USDA reference.
Surfaces and shells affect the usable weight

If a trail mix recipe calls for 14 g of each, the combined handful has around 3.9 g protein and 17.0 g fat. Count pistachio weight after shelling when doing the calculation. A bag’s out-of-shell and in-shell weights describe different amounts of edible food.
Keep the flavor label nearby if you want to compare added salt. The numbers here refer to the plain raw nuts.
table: Two raw nut servings by edible weight

article: How different are cooked couscous and amaranth in protein?
Put the two cooked pantry staples on the same weight basis and check fiber separately.
USDA SR Legacy cooked couscous and cooked amaranth. Water-only comparison of edible cooked portions.
copy: At 160 g cooked, couscous and amaranth each contribute about 6.1 g protein in these USDA records. Amaranth gives around 3.4 g fiber, compared with 2.2 g for couscous. Matching protein here happens to use the same cooked weight.
Compare the base before the toppings

Choose the exact grain and preparation. Dry package weights describe a different amount because cooking adds water. Pearl couscous, a sauce-coated amaranth bowl or a ready-to-heat blend would need its own entry before you compare portions.
These numbers describe the plain base. Pile toppings on two matched bases if you want to see which addition changes the whole meal most.
